question: If you must ride over an obstacle you cannot avoid, the manual says you should approach it at as close to what angle as possible?
choice_d: It doesn't matter what angle you use
explanation: If you have to ride over an obstacle, approach it at as close to a 90-degree angle as possible, and look where you want to go to control your path of travel.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.26, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: Just before riding over an unavoidable obstacle, the manual recommends rising slightly off the seat with your weight on the footpegs and:
choice_a: Rolling on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end just before contact
choice_b: Closing the throttle completely and coasting over it
choice_c: Applying the front brake through the entire obstacle
choice_d: Sitting down firmly to add weight to both wheels
explanation: Rise slightly off the seat with your weight on the footpegs to absorb the shock with your knees and elbows, and just before contact, roll on the throttle slightly to lighten the front end.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.26, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: After riding over an object in the street, the manual says you should:
choice_a: Continue riding normally unless the motorcycle starts to shake
choice_c: Only check the motorcycle once you reach your final destination
choice_d: Pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther
explanation: If you ride over an object on the street, pull off the road and check your tires and rims for damage before riding any farther.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.26-27, 'Uneven Surfaces and Obstacles'

question: The manual lists wet pavement as most slippery:
choice_a: Only after several hours of continuous rain
choice_b: Particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road
choice_d: It is equally slippery at all points during rain
explanation: Surfaces that provide poor traction include wet pavement, particularly just after it starts to rain and before surface oil washes to the side of the road.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: Which of the following is NOT listed by the manual as a poor-traction surface?
choice_a: Lane markings, steel plates, and manhole covers, especially when wet
choice_b: Gravel roads, or where sand and gravel collect
choice_c: Freshly applied dry asphalt with no markings
explanation: Poor-traction surfaces listed include wet pavement, gravel roads or where sand and gravel collect, mud/snow/ice, and lane markings, steel plates, and manhole covers especially when wet -- not plain dry asphalt.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: To ride safely on slippery surfaces, the manual advises being smooth and avoiding:
choice_a: Any sudden change in speed or direction, which can cause a skid
choice_b: Using the front brake under any circumstances
choice_c: Shifting gears at all until the surface ends
explanation: Avoid sudden moves -- any sudden change in speed or direction can cause a skid. Be as smooth as possible when you speed up, shift gears, turn, or brake.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: On a slippery surface, the manual says the front brake:
choice_a: Should never be used under any circumstances
choice_b: Should be applied as hard as possible for the shortest stopping distance
choice_d: Is still effective if you squeeze the lever gradually to avoid locking the front wheel
explanation: Use both brakes -- the front brake is still effective, even on a slippery surface. Squeeze the brake lever gradually to avoid locking the front wheel, and use gentle pressure on the rear brake.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: When it starts to rain, the manual suggests riding in which part of the lane, since the center can be hazardous when wet?
choice_a: The far left edge of the road, off the pavement
choice_b: The tire tracks left by cars
choice_c: Directly on the center oil strip
choice_d: It makes no difference where you ride once it rains
explanation: The center of a lane can be hazardous when wet. When it starts to rain, ride in the tire tracks left by cars -- often the left tire track will be less oily.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: The manual notes that patches of ice tend to crop up in low or shaded areas and on:
explanation: Rain dries and snow melts faster on some sections of a road than on others. Patches of ice tend to crop up in low or shaded areas and on bridges and overpasses.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: If you encounter a large, very slippery surface that forces you to coast at a walking pace, the manual advises you to:
choice_a: Keep the motorcycle straight, stay off the brakes, and consider letting your feet skim the surface
choice_b: Apply the front brake continuously to maintain control
choice_c: Accelerate through it as quickly as possible
choice_d: Lean the motorcycle sharply to one side for balance
explanation: If you encounter a large surface so slippery you must coast or travel at a walking pace, keep the motorcycle straight up, be sure to keep off the brakes, and consider letting your feet skim along the surface so you can catch yourself if the motorcycle starts to fall.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.27, 'Slippery Surfaces'

question: According to the manual, when crossing railroad or trolley tracks that run across your path, it is usually safer to:
choice_a: Always turn to cross every set of tracks at a full 90-degree angle
choice_b: Change lanes immediately before every crossing
choice_c: Accelerate hard the moment you see tracks ahead
choice_d: Ride straight within your lane, rather than turning to take the tracks head-on at a 90-degree angle
explanation: Usually it is safer to ride straight within your lane to cross tracks. Turning to take tracks head-on (at a 90-degree angle) can be more dangerous -- your path may carry you into another lane of traffic.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.28, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: For tracks or pavement seams that run parallel to your course, the manual says you should move far enough away to cross at an angle of at least:
choice_b: 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn
choice_d: There is no recommended minimum angle
explanation: For track and road seams that run parallel to your course, move far enough away from tracks, ruts, or pavement seams to cross at an angle of at least 45 degrees, then make a deliberate turn -- edging across could catch your tires and throw you off balance.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.28, 'Railroad Tracks, Trolley Tracks and Pavement Seams'

question: When riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings that cause the motorcycle to weave, the manual advises you to:
choice_a: Brake immediately to reduce the weaving sensation
choice_b: Zigzag to find a smoother path
choice_c: Relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across
choice_d: Accelerate hard to power through the weave
explanation: Riding over rain grooves or bridge gratings may cause a motorcycle to weave. The uneasy, wandering feeling is generally not hazardous. Relax, maintain a steady speed, and ride straight across.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.28, 'Grooves and Gratings'

question: The manual says crossing grooves or gratings at an angle, forcing riders to zigzag to stay in the lane, is:
choice_a: Far more hazardous than the wandering feeling of riding straight across
choice_c: Required whenever the grating is wet
explanation: Crossing at an angle forces riders to zigzag to stay in the lane. The zigzag is far more hazardous than the wandering feeling of riding straight across.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.28, 'Grooves and Gratings'
